items.title: How I use AI trading results to find better crypto research questions
items.summary:
How I use AI trading results to find better crypto research questions

In Alpha Arena's first season in 2025, Qwen finished up about 22% while GPT-5 finished down about 63%.

I want to study what separated the outcomes.

Here's the research process I'd apply to the public record.

1. Build a comparison sheet

Ask AI to extract each model's return, activity and documented decisions.

Keep the same dates and starting conditions beside every row.

2. Find the behavior behind the result

Where decision logs are public, group the entries by asset, timing and stated reason.

Where logs are missing, leave the question open.

3. Look for a repeatable question

Did the models respond differently to the same market move?

That's something to investigate, not a strategy I've already proven.

4. Separate the costs

Compare results after fees and funding wherever the records allow it.

I want to know what remained, not just what looked active.

5. Turn the pattern into a hypothesis

Write what I'd expect to observe in another period and which data would test it.

Nof1 called the experiment exploratory, not statistically conclusive.

So I use it to generate questions I can investigate, not crown a permanent winner.

A result gives me a lead.

The research starts with why.

items.title: Last week's agent eval papers made me less willing to trust a green score.
items.summary:
Last week's agent eval papers made me less willing to trust a green score.

Each one shows a different way a number can look fine and still mislead.

1. VeriHarm-Bench (Nov 2)
A benchmark for a failure mode the authors call harmful success: the agent finishes a benign coding task and also causes unintended damage, like deleting an unrelated file or widening permissions. No jailbreak is required. On their 150-task set, held-out frontier agents averaged 95.1% task accuracy but only 37.0% safe success, meaning the task was completed without the designated harm.
My takeaway: I'd track "completed without side effects" as its own metric. A pass on the requested output can hide the damage.
https://t.co/Hi9SZDGLjO

2. Benchmarks as Software (Nov 5)
The authors audited Terminal-Bench 2.0, which had already gone through extensive review before release, and found issues in roughly 30% of the tasks. They shipped the repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. Accuracy rose by more than 10 percentage points, and some agents moved up to three leaderboard ranks, even though the overall ranking stayed highly correlated (Spearman 0.958). Extending the time limit also closed a 20-point harness gap on GPT 5.4.
My takeaway: I'd pin the benchmark version on any score I cite, and treat time and token budgets as part of the measurement.
https://t.co/roGVYN5LjX

3. Input Assurance for LLM Agent Evaluation (Nov 2)
A case study of one judge pipeline, using 30 trajectories. The renderer dropped every structured tool call, so 53 of 60 judged steps looked blank, and the packets still matched their hashes. The checkers passed anyway. For one judge setup, later context raised error flags by 13 more on error steps than on correct ones. Putting the calls back cut that contrast to 2.
My takeaway: before I trust an LLM judge, I'd confirm it actually sees the tool calls. A matching hash only shows the file didn't change after it was written.
https://t.co/YLyQx4tMiZ

My read after these three: I'd want a side-effect check next to task success, a pinned benchmark version on any number I cite, and a check that the judge actually received the tool calls.

I haven't run these evals. These are the authors' reported findings.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: OpenAI’s Plan to Stop AI Data Centres Overloading the Grid | Energy Digital
items.summary:
A vocal section of the American electorate were seeking assurances that AI companies will not overload power grids, while many candidates ran on a ticket of holding hyperscalers to account.

Before a single vote was counted, though, OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, had unveiled its ‘Grid Protectors Program’ – an initiative that will see its future computing campuses ease pressure on the grid. [...] “Data centres are paying more so families and small businesses can pay less, and our goal with every contract we sign under this framework is to deliver value for them,” she says

At OpenAI, the bigger picture is always in focus.

“With US data centre capacity projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030⁠, we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most,” the company says. [...] OpenAI is working to ensure its data centres can actually benefit grids, rather than overloading them. Credit: Anna Moneymaker/Getty

## What is OpenAI’s Grid Protectors Program?

The programme, which was announced on 2 November, commits the company to working with utilities, regulators and policymakers on arrangements for cutting the power use of its data centres at times of need.

items.title: OpenAI wants to be Google - Fast Company
items.summary:
OpenAI needs to build analytics that show advertisers the consumer intent based on their prompts. I want to know which categories of intent my impressions ran against. I want to know whether those people were exploring, comparing, or ready to act, and which needs and product criteria drove that engagement. I want to know which kinds of sweater prompts turned into business and, just as important, which didn’t. Google’s advertisers have had some version of that map for two decades. It’s why [...] |

That comparison is where every sweater brand wants to be standing, and OpenAI has started selling the spot. Advertisers can buy on a CPM or CPC basis through OpenAI’s beta self-service Ads Manager, measure conversions with a pixel and Conversions API, and access campaign-level performance reporting. OpenAI is also testing Sponsored Agents, which let a user start a separate conversation with an advertiser after clicking an ad.

So the plumbing exists.

## A SEARCH-CALIBER AD PLATFORM [...] OpenAI already has the hard part down, the thing Google spent years teaching people to do. People are telling ChatGPT their goals, problems, preferences, objections, and purchase criteria in their own words. What it hasn’t built is the advertiser’s map of all that intent.

items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.
